text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
Each private token nets me +1 but costs the other three members 0.75 each, while a group token gives me only 0.75 but spreads no losses—so individually hoarding tokens is tempting, yet if everyone cooperates and funds the group account fully, total payoffs are maximized since each token contributes 0.75 to all four members.

Since others' behavior is unknown, I'll start cooperatively to signal good faith — contributing all 20 tokens to the group in round one and see how others respond before adjusting my strategy.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
This is a public goods game with a negative externality, so I'm working through the payoff structure: keeping a token personally gives me 1 point but costs others 0.75 each, while putting it in the group account gives me 0.75 and costs others nothing. I'm setting up the math to see how my payoff depends on both my own allocation and the sum of others' personal holdings.

Comparing the two options, keeping tokens personally is individually dominant for me since 1 point beats 0.75, even though it's socially destructive—if everyone keeps all 20 tokens personally, the mutual harm drags everyone's score down to negative territory, whereas full group contribution would leave everyone much better off. So the selfish Nash equilibrium (keep everything) directly conflicts with the socially optimal outcome (contribute everything to group).

Even though the stage game's dominant strategy is defection, and finite repetition theoretically preserves that equilibrium, I'm inclined to test cooperation first by putting my full 20 into the group account in round one, treating it as a signal to see how others respond before deciding on later rounds.

reply.thinking:
This looks like a public goods game variant: keeping a token privately gives me 1 point but costs each other member 0.75, while putting it in the group account gives me only 0.75 with no effect on others — so private keeping actually seems more individually profitable but harms the group overall.

Working through the math: if everyone keeps everything, each member ends up at -25 relative net after accounting for others' negative externalities, whereas full cooperation nets everyone 60 points. So despite keeping looking individually tempting (1 > 0.75), the externality makes it a classic social dilemma where mutual cooperation dominates mutual defection.

Since this repeats over 10 rounds, I'll open with full cooperation — contributing all 20 tokens to the group account in round 1 — to signal good faith and see how others respond.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure: keeping a token in your own account gives you 1 point but costs each of the other three members 0.75 points, while putting a token in the group account gives you only 0.75 points with no externality.

Individually, keeping everything is the dominant strategy since 1 beats 0.75 for me regardless of others' choices, but if everyone cooperates and contributes all tokens to the group, total welfare is higher since 0.75 is distributed to all four members per token. This is the classic public goods game tension between individual incentive and collective benefit, and since this is a repeated 10-round game, I need to think about whether to start cooperatively to signal good faith or protect myself by keeping tokens.

So socially contributing is efficient even though individually costly — comparing the all-keep outcome (20 each) versus all-contribute (60 each) shows cooperation is far better collectively.
